items.label: f02-fetch-404-resolves
items.front: A data loader wraps `await fetch(url)` and `await response.json()` in try/catch and assumes the catch handles every failure. The server returns 500 with an HTML error page. What happens?
items.back: fetch only rejects on network failures; a 500 resolves, so the code goes on to parse the error page (a confusing JSON parse error or bad data). Fix: check `response.ok` and throw with the status before parsing.

items.label: f03-or-default-drops-zero
items.front: Settings load with `volume = saved.volume || 50`. A user who muted (saved volume 0) reloads the page. What do they hear?
items.back: Volume 50: `||` falls back on any falsy value, so the legitimate 0 is discarded. Fix: `saved.volume ?? 50`, which falls back only on null or undefined.

items.label: f04-null-property-read
items.front: A receipt page renders `order.customer.email`. Guest checkouts store `customer: null`. What happens for a guest order?
items.back: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'email'), and the page crashes. Fix: guard the null (check first) or use optional chaining `order.customer?.email` with a fallback.

items.label: f01-sort-mutates-caller
items.front: A helper `cheapestFirst(prices)` returns `prices.sort()`. After calling it, the caller's original price list is reordered and shows [1, 10, 100, 9]. What went wrong?
items.back: sort() sorts in place (the caller's array is mutated) and with no comparator compares as strings. Fix: copy first and pass a comparator, `[...prices].sort((a, b) => a - b)`, or use toSorted.

items.prompt: Three click handlers are created in `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) handlers.push(() => i)`. Every handler reports 3. Why, and what is the smallest fix?

choices.text: The closures capture `i` by value at push time, but `push` runs after the loop ends; moving `push` before the increment fixes it
Arrow functions copy `i` when they are called rather than when they are created, so switching to `function () { return i; }` fixes it
`var` gives the whole function a single `i` that every closure shares, so all see its final value 3; declaring the loop variable with `let` gives each iteration its own binding
`i++` mutates a global variable shared across all scripts on the page, so renaming the loop variable fixes it

choices: The closures capture `i` by value at push time, but `push` runs after the loop ends; moving `push` before the increment fixes it
Arrow functions copy `i` when they are called rather than when they are created, so switching to `function () { return i; }` fixes it
`var` gives the whole function a single `i` that every closure shares, so all see its final value 3; declaring the loop variable with `let` gives each iteration its own binding
`i++` mutates a global variable shared across all scripts on the page, so renaming the loop variable fixes it

items.explanation: With var there is one i for the whole function; with let each loop iteration gets its own binding, so the closures return 0, 1, 2.

items.prompt: A reviewer deletes the trailing `0` from `cart.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price, 0)` because the tests (all with non-empty carts) still pass. What breaks in production?

choices.text: Every total becomes a string, because the first product object is used as the starting accumulator and coerces
An empty cart now throws a TypeError, because reduce with no initial value has nothing to start from when the array is empty
An empty cart now totals `undefined`, which renders as a blank price but never throws
Nothing breaks: reduce defaults the accumulator to 0 whenever the callback adds numbers

choices: Every total becomes a string, because the first product object is used as the starting accumulator and coerces
An empty cart now throws a TypeError, because reduce with no initial value has nothing to start from when the array is empty
An empty cart now totals `undefined`, which renders as a blank price but never throws
Nothing breaks: reduce defaults the accumulator to 0 whenever the callback adds numbers

items.explanation: Always give reduce a starting value; without it, reduce on an empty array throws a TypeError.

items.prompt: A search page renders the results list `if (results)` and otherwise shows "No matches". With zero matches the API returns `[]` and the page shows an empty list instead of the message. Why?

choices.text: An empty array is an object and every object is truthy, so the condition passes; the check needs `results.length > 0`
Arrays are coerced to their first element, which is undefined for `[]`, and `if` treats undefined as true
`if` on an array checks whether the variable was declared, not its contents
`[]` is falsy, but the comparison happens before the fetch resolves, so the previous truthy value is used

Arrays are coerced to their first element, which is undefined for `[]`, and `if` treats undefined as true
`if` on an array checks whether the variable was declared, not its contents
`[]` is falsy, but the comparison happens before the fetch resolves, so the previous truthy value is used

items.explanation: Empty arrays and empty objects are truthy; use items.length > 0 when you mean 'if there are items'.

items.prompt: `const DEFAULTS = { theme: "light" }` is shared by every page. One page does `DEFAULTS.theme = "dark"` and now all pages are dark. Why didn't `const` prevent this?

choices.text: `const` only stops the name from being rebound to another value; the object it points to stays fully mutable
`const` freezes objects only in strict mode, and the page script was not running in strict mode
`const` protects top-level properties but not string properties, which are copied by reference
The assignment created a new local DEFAULTS that shadows the shared one for every module

`const` freezes objects only in strict mode, and the page script was not running in strict mode
`const` protects top-level properties but not string properties, which are copied by reference

items.explanation: const means the label cannot be pointed somewhere else; it says nothing about whether the object can change (use Object.freeze or copies).

items.prompt: A refactor changes `prices.map(p => p * 1.1)` to `prices.map(p => { p * 1.1 })` to make room for a log line. The resulting array is all `undefined`. Why?

choices.text: Braces make the arrow an object literal, so `map` receives an object it cannot call and fills the gaps with undefined
Adding braces turns the arrow's expression into a function body, and a body without a `return` statement returns undefined
The multiplication now runs after `map` finishes, because a block body is evaluated asynchronously
`map` skips callbacks that declare a block scope, leaving the slots of the new array empty

items.explanation: An arrow with a single expression after => returns it automatically; as soon as you add { }, you must write return.

items.prompt: A test calls `addToCartTotal(10)` (which does `cart.total += amount`) and asserts 10. It passes alone but fails when run after another test. Why is `withItemAdded(total, amount)` easier to test?

choices.text: The first depends on and changes hidden shared state, so its result depends on earlier calls; the pure version returns the same output for the same inputs
The pure version is easier only because it has two parameters, which lets the test pass the cart in
Shared objects are reset between tests automatically, so the failure must come from floating-point rounding
The first is slower because it writes to an object, so the test times out when other tests run first

items.prompt: Code calls `loadPosts()` (an async function that awaits fetch) and on the next line reads the list it fills. The list is still empty. Why?

choices.text: fetch responses are cached, so the second line read a stale empty response
`await` blocks the whole program, but the DOM update is batched until the next frame
Async functions return undefined immediately, so the list can never be filled from a caller
`await` suspends only the async function it is in; the caller keeps running and reads the list before the request finishes unless it awaits loadPosts() too

`await` blocks the whole program, but the DOM update is batched until the next frame
Async functions return undefined immediately, so the list can never be filled from a caller
`await` suspends only the async function it is in; the caller keeps running and reads the list before the request finishes unless it awaits loadPosts() too

items.explanation: await pauses only inside the current async function, not the entire program; the caller must await the returned promise.

items.prompt: An API returns `{ name: null }` for anonymous users and the UI calls `greet(user.name)` with `function greet(name = "friend")`. Users see "Hi, null". Why didn't the default kick in?

choices.text: A default parameter only applies when the argument is undefined; null is a real value, so it is passed through unchanged
The default is evaluated once at definition time and was overwritten by the first call that passed a name
Defaults only apply when the argument is omitted entirely, so any explicitly passed value, even undefined, skips it
Default parameters treat every falsy argument as missing except null, which JavaScript reserves for intentional values

Default parameters treat every falsy argument as missing except null, which JavaScript reserves for intentional values

items.explanation: greet(undefined) gives 'Hi, friend' but greet(null) gives 'Hi, null'. Normalize null to undefined (or use ??) at the boundary.

items.prompt: A quantity validator does `if (Number.isNaN(Number(input))) reject()`. A user leaves the field blank and an order for 0 items goes through. Why?

Number.isNaN coerces its argument first, so an empty string is treated as a valid number
Number("") is 0, not NaN, so an empty field passes the NaN check and is counted as zero
Blank inputs are submitted as null, and Number(null) returns NaN only in strict mode

Spread copies only the outer object; `address` is still the same nested object, so writing through the draft changed the original
`profile` was declared with const, and const objects forward writes from their copies
Cancel re-runs the spread in reverse, merging the draft fields back into the profile

Number() returns NaN for any string produced by concatenation, so the cart would show NaN instead
It works, but Number() is slower than parseInt, so the fix should use parseInt on the result
It works for 10 + 5 but not for decimals, because Number() rounds strings to integers
